newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Hasina government draws fire over highway plan.
newsitem.headline: Hasina government draws fire over highway plan.

text.p: Bangladesh opposition parties, suspicious of India, are mounting a campaign against proposals for an Asian Highway cutting across the country.

The government is sending Communication Minister Anwar Hossain Manju to New Delhi this week for a United Nations conference on the proposed Highway, which would stretch from Turkey to China by way of a dozen central, south and southeast Asian countries.
But while Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina hopes to improve impoverished Bangladesh's links with the outside world, former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia, smells a plot.

"A conspiracy is underway to give India a land transit over Bangladesh in the name of linkage to the Asian Highway," Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan secretary-general of Khaleda's Bangladesh Nationalist Party, said it a recent statement.

Smaller opposition groups issued similar warnings of resistance, including a vow from the Jatiya Ganatantrik of Shafiul Alam Pradhan that its members would sacrifice their blood rather than yield over transit rights.
The plan could "lead Bangladesh into quicksand," Dhaka's Inquilab newspaper warned on Sunday.
For India the road could be a shortcut to its isolated northeastern states, which lie east of Bangladesh and are linked to the rest of India only by a roundabout northern corridor.
Bangladesh opposition parties say it would "open up the country to India's hegemonist designs."

The government promises that it would not do anything that goes against national interest but, in the words of Sheikh Hasina, "We can't afford to remain disconnected with other countries in this modern world."
Manju told Reuters last week that "We are eager to hook up our communication system with the rest of the world. It's in the interest of our trade and tourism.
"We have been like an island for decades. This is a trend against the time. It should end," he said.
Some 20 Asian countries are expected to attend the Delhi conference sponsored by ESCAP, the U.N.'s Bangkok-based Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific.
The idea of a highway to boost trade and tourism among Asian countries dates back to the 1960s and has recently been revived.

Communication Ministry officials said the highway might to enter Bangladesh from Burma through the frontier district of Cox's Bazar and connect with India through the southwestern district of Jessore.
